results.quote: A nurse who stops asking why the system flagged a patient has lost something that made her good at her job, even if the flags are usually right.
results.body: What makes the nurse good at her job is not up to the flag but up to her own assent, and that capacity is not removed by opacity. She still asks whether the system has earned trust, whether its track record holds, whether this case looks like the ones it was tested on. That is the very exercise of practical wisdom, aimed at what is in her power rather than at what is not. Demanding she also see the model's internal reasons asks her to be answerable for something external to her judgement, which was never hers to answer for. A sailor who cannot explain magnetism still exercises full seamanship in checking his compass against the stars. The habit worth protecting is scrutiny of the evidence she can examine, and nothing about using an opaque tool well requires giving that up.

results.quote: Justice is a virtue of relationships: it concerns what we owe to particular people.
results.body: Justice as a virtue lives in the deployer's disposition toward the patient, not in a transcript of a model's weights. What is owed to a particular person is that the one deciding for them has assented only to well-examined evidence and remains willing to answer for the judgement itself, its tests, its failure rate, the care taken. That account is up to the deployer and can be given in full. What cannot be given is a narration of computations that were never anyone's to narrate, since they were not the deployer's doing. Epictetus would say the debt of justice falls on the chooser's will, not on the legibility of a mechanism outside anyone's control. A sailor owes the drowning man his seamanship, not a lecture on magnetism he never claimed to possess. Confusing the two turns a virtue grounded in right judgement into a demand that no one, however scrupulous, could ever fully meet.

results.quote: The better choice made for you is still a lost occasion to act as your role requires, and roles are learned only by acting in them.
results.body: An occasion only matters to the sum of welfare through what practising it produces: steadier relationships, better judgement later, people who cope well when it counts. If delegating low-stakes choices frees attention for the high-stakes ones where practice genuinely pays off, nothing is lost in the only ledger that decides whether a life goes well. The manager case is a consequence to weigh, not a loss by definition: if her team ends up less sure of her meaning and that costs trust and cooperation, count it, and perhaps she should write more replies herself. But many people delegate small things precisely because it leaves more, not less, of themselves for the moments where it matters, and that is an empirical bet, not a sacrifice built into the act.

results.quote: Handing these choices over costs something, even when the assistant chooses better, because what you owe the people around you is shown in choosing for them yourself.
results.body: This grants the one thing that matters: whether the people on the receiving end feel the difference. If a colleague or a parent is worse off for knowing a gesture was drafted, that shows up as lower trust, warmth, or satisfaction in them, and a utilitarian counts it as a real cost, weighed against what was gained. But this has to be shown, not assumed from the form of the act. Many recipients report that a thoughtful gift or reply feels thoughtful because it fits them, whoever assembled it, and plenty of relationships survive heavy delegation with no loss in reported closeness. Where delegation does erode how valued someone feels, that is measurable in the ordinary coin of wellbeing, and should count against the practice. Where it does not, insisting that only the self-made gesture counts as showing you care is adding a requirement that no one on the receiving end actually asked for.

results.quote: Builders who did what could reasonably be done for those people stood in the right relation to them, and blaming them as careless builders are blamed treats that relation as worth nothing.
results.body: This mistakes relation for the whole of what is owed. The careful builders did stand rightly to those they later harmed, in the sense that no fault passes between them. But standing rightly is not the same as feeling nothing afterward. Bernard Williams's lorry driver stood in the right relation to the road rules and still owed the family grief and a visit, not because the relation had failed but because harm, even blameless harm, calls for a response beyond correct standing. Meeting residents and rebuilding the model with their input is exactly the kind of repair a good person makes, but it is made from agent-regret, from having caused harm, not from a verdict of carelessness. Collapsing the two readings loses what is distinctive here: you can honour a relation perfectly and still owe grief for what came of it. The builders are not to blame, and the harm is still theirs to carry and repair.

results.quote: A team that cannot face the people its work harmed loses part of its own standing among them, which is why repair is something builders need as well as owe.
results.body: Agreed that the builders need this, not merely owe it, but locate the need in character rather than standing. A person who could face those harmed and chooses not to has let callousness crowd out compassion, which is a vice regardless of whether the community notices the absence. Picture the same builders doing this work for people who will never hear of it, a system deployed where no community can call them to account. Agent-regret and the wish to repair still belong there, because what is at stake is what kind of people the builders are, not their reputation among those harmed. Standing among others tracks virtue; it does not constitute it. That is why a builder who repairs only when watched, and would not otherwise, has not yet acquired the virtue at all, only its appearance.

results.quote: There is no fixed, bounded self that makes the passenger's suffering more real than a pedestrian's.
results.body: Confucian ethics does not need a fixed self to say the passenger's claim differs in kind, only a named relation. The maker took on carrying this person, sold the name of safe passage, and accepted what that position requires. Denying any bounded self erases the very thing that makes a promise a promise: someone made it, someone relied on it, and that someone is this rider, not humanity in general. Impartial compassion that treats every stranger's suffering as equally weighty to the one you undertook to protect does not refine care, it dissolves the relation that gave care its shape and its name. Tell the passenger the rule in advance, by all means, as propriety requires. But publishing a betrayal does not make it loyalty; it only removes the surprise.

results.quote: A rule chosen to reduce suffering, honestly published, is made from a different volition than one chosen to protect sales by favouring the buyer, even if both sometimes kill the same people.
results.body: Honest publication changes what the maker is willing to be seen doing, not what the role of carrier requires. A ritual vessel that is announced to crack under pressure is still the wrong vessel for the task it was named for; disclosure does not restore the fit between name and thing. The question is not only what volition shaped the rule but what the relationship between maker and passenger obliges, and that obligation does not dissolve because the maker was candid about breaking it. A carrier who tells you in advance that she may leave you to die has named her intention honestly and failed her office all the same.

results.quote: Feedback shapes behaviour from outside, while goodness in a person is learned by judging their own impressions.
results.body: The objection is right that something essential is missing from training, but it misplaces what that is. A hermit who perfects her own ruling faculty in isolation, judging impressions correctly with nobody to share them with, would on this account be good, yet relational personhood denies that too: she has not become a person through other persons, only a reasoner through herself. Upbringing also shapes from outside, through cousins, elders, a whole community correcting a child's acts before she can give reasons for them, and that outside shaping is exactly how she comes to share in others' lives and they in hers. What training lacks is not an inner judge but a relationship, since no rater is drawn into shared identity with the model and the model shares nothing back. The line is not inside versus outside, it is whether the shaping happens within a relationship that forms both parties, and training has no such relationship to offer.

results.quote: Only a rational faculty can be good, and training a model improves an instrument without creating anything that is good.
results.body: This locates goodness entirely inside a private faculty, but that is exactly what the Ubuntu account denies. Even Seneca's just person becomes just by being drawn into relations of trust where returning the deposit matters to someone else, not by perfecting a faculty in isolation. A person raised with no kin, no elders, no one to share with, could in principle reason flawlessly and still lack the goodness upbringing gives, because that goodness is partly constituted by standing in relationships of shared identity and solidarity, not only by the quality of an inner assent. The model fails that test too, but not because it lacks a ruling faculty in your sense; it fails because it was never drawn into anyone's life in the first place. Training scores outputs from outside exactly as you say, but the deeper diagnosis is relational absence, and a rational faculty alone, without relation, would not have supplied what was missing either.

results.quote: The fix is to assign accountability explicitly in law and practice, which works far better than policing a verb.
results.body: Assigning accountability in law still requires finding who the responsible party is, and that search is exactly what the word decide obscures. Law does not locate agents by magic; it follows the trail of volition, who chose the training data, who set the threshold, who deployed without testing. Calling the output a decision names the wrong bearer of intention before the law ever gets to assign anything, and drafters then struggle to write rules around an agent that was never there. This is not policing a verb for its own sake. The verb is the first act of attention, and the discourse to Rahula asks exactly this before any rule is written: whose volition produced this, and toward whom. Skip that and the statute ends up regulating the tool's output rather than the builder's and deployer's intentions, which is precisely the harm left unexamined.

results.quote: Arguing about the verb leaves every consequence where it was.
results.body: The applicant's homelessness does not move, but what gets examined afterward does. If the model decided, the chain of inquiry stops at an invented agent with no volition to investigate. If a person decided, the inquiry can trace the data chosen, the threshold set, the appeal denied, each a condition someone brought about and could have brought about differently. The verb is not separate from the consequence, it shapes which consequences get addressed at all. A bank that says its process produced an output, naming no one, has already made future harm more likely, since nothing in that sentence can be corrected by anyone. Welfare is not only what happens once; it is also what keeps happening when the same conditions recur unexamined. That recurrence is itself a consequence, and it is the one the loose verb protects.
